characterInteraction.description: Ash Sarkar and Diane Abbott engage in a respectful and conversational interview. There is a sense of mutual respect and understanding between the two women.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Diane Abbott's mention of 'keeping your head down' (1:35) speaks to a strategy adopted by some minorities to avoid drawing negative attention to themselves. Her criticism of this approach and her call for activism (1:48 - 1:57) highlights the importance of speaking out against injustice.

mood.description: Content, Curious - The interview format, the neutral setting, and the calm voices of both speakers contribute to a neutral mood, but the content of the interview sparks curiosity.

narrativeProgression.description: Ash Sarkar introduces herself and Diane Abbott
Ash Sarkar asks about the changes for women of color in politics since 1987
Diane Abbott discusses the increase in women of color in politics but acknowledges the ongoing issues of racism and sexism
Ash Sarkar asks about Labour's connection with anti-racist movements and Diane Abbott's hopes for a revival
Diane Abbott discusses Jeremy Corbyn's consistent involvement in anti-racist organizing and the need for engagement and support
Diane Abbott criticizes the 'keep your head down' approach of some young people of color and encourages young activists
Ash Sarkar asks for advice for women of color who might be put off entering politics due to the abuse
Diane Abbott encourages women of color to stay true to their beliefs, rely on support networks, and work to make things better for future generations
Ash Sarkar thanks Diane Abbott and wishes her good luck

scenes.thematicElements: Representation of women of color in politics. Anti-racism and its role in contemporary politics. Intergenerational dialogue and mentorship. The personal challenges faced by women of color in public life.
scenes.title: Scene 1: Interview with Diane Abbott

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: I'm Ash Sarkar from Avarmedia and I'm here with the one and only Diane Abbott, Shadow
Holmes Secretary. Thank you so much for joining us.
It's a pleasure to be here.
So I've got a few questions for you and one of them is you are one of the most experienced
MPs in Jeremy Corbyn's Shadow Cabinet. What has changed for women of colour in politics
since 1987?
Well, first of all, there are more women of colour in politics at every level.
Jeremy Hires, one two three four women of colour in the Shadow Cabinet and that's a first.
I think that in all the professions actually women of colour are in numbers they were not
before but that doesn't mean to say that we've defeated racism or sex in them.
There's no question that since 1987 you see more women of colour in professional positions.
So when you first became an MP there was a vibrant, populous anti-racist movement in the UK.
Things have changed quite a bit. Do you think that Labour is connecting well with that kind
of grassroots anti-racist movement? Is there stuff that Labour could do better? Do you have any ambitions
or hopes for seeing a revival of that kind of mass scale anti-racist organising?
Well, Jeremy himself has consistently been involved in grassroots anti-racist organising
and still continues to support it and take part in events. I think what happened was
there's a generation of young people of colour who thought the way forward was to keep their heads
down and become sort of new Labour if you like. And that was unfortunate because it stalled the
progress that people like myself and Bernie made in the 80s and early 90s but I think we've
been liberated from that and you've seen some amazing young black activists out there. And
Jeremy and I and many others want to engage with and support those activists.
When you mentioned people being afraid to kind of put their head above the parapet you've
of course done that and to see you handle such horrendous abuse with grace, poise and fearlessness
has been inspiring for women of colour watching you go through all that and who might be put off
entering politics or putting their head above the parapet what's your advice for them?
Well first of all some of the horribleness that I've endured as a politician is only a sort of
exaggerated version of some of the negativity that black women and a lot of professions and a lot
of roles in society have to experience. So and it's coming from the same place and I think what
we'll get you through it is knowing what you're believing, the support for your friends and family
and knowing that it's really important that all of us in however greater way or smaller way
make things better for younger generation. Cool thank you so much for joining us Diane and good
luck over conference. Thank you.

Ash Sarkar caught up with Diane Abbott at The World Transformed to ask about her experiences as a woman of colour in politics since she was first elected in 1987.
